Koprivnica Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Koprivnica, Croatia

Not demolished. Koprivnica, a northern Croatian town whose castle was first mentioned in 1272, became a major regional administrative and trading center by the 14th century. Jews arrived from Moravia and Austria in the late 17th century; by 1810, 23 Jews worked mainly in crafts, trade, and agriculture, later becoming prominent industrialists - Jewish management ran the 'Deniza' plant, which employed 600 workers. A formal community organized by the mid-19th century, building a Renaissance-style synagogue in 1875 (designed by Hönigsberg and Deutsch) alongside a German-language Jewish school; the community was overwhelmingly Ashkenazi, with only 3 Sephardic families. Jewish population reached 398 by 1896. During the Holocaust, Croatian nationalists deported most of Koprivnica's 358 prewar Jews to concentration camps; 214 deaths are documented, with the rest unaccounted for, and the community's last rabbi, Israel Kohn, was tortured in a camp. The synagogue - one of few in Croatia to survive the war - was sold to the municipality in 1948 and renovated into a concert hall in 2013. This cemetery, built 3km from town in 1842 (Hevra Kadisha founded 1888), holds tombstones from 1836 to 2017, including five family mausoleums, inscriptions in Hebrew, German, Croatian, and some Hungarian, a WWI soldiers' memorial, and a 1975 Holocaust monument. Its ceremonial hall was recently reconstructed as a Holocaust memorial.
